title: Mumbai Gets Its First Dedicated Wine Bar as Pique Opens in South Mumbai's Horniman Circle
excerpt: Founded by Le Cordon Bleu graduate Sasha Goenka, the two-level wine bar aims to make wine culture an everyday habit in a city that has embraced craft beer and specialty coffee but not yet the grape.
body:
• Pique, a new two-level wine bar and kitchen at Horniman Circle in South Mumbai, aims to make wine an everyday habit rather than a special-occasion drink.
  • Founded by Sasha Goenka, a Le Cordon Bleu Paris graduate with WSET Level 3 certification, the venue offers 12 wines by the glass and 24 by the bottle, refreshed monthly.
  • An exclusive partnership with Vallonne Vineyards features one of the few Indian orange wines currently available by the glass at any restaurant in the country.
  • The food menu, created with chef and cheesemaker Aditya Raghavan, focuses on European-inspired sharing plates made with locally sourced Indian ingredients.

Mumbai has spent the past decade falling hard for specialty coffee and craft beer. Wine, though, has remained the awkward guest at the party — something ordered at hotel bars or saved for celebrations. Sasha Goenka wants to change that.

Her new venture, Pique, is a two-level wine bar and kitchen tucked into the heritage precinct of Horniman Circle in South Mumbai. It opened in late July with a straightforward pitch: wine should feel like a Tuesday habit, not a black-tie obligation.

A Wine-First Concept for a Beer-and-Cocktails City

Goenka brings serious credentials to the project. She is a Le Cordon Bleu Paris graduate with WSET Level 3 certification — the globally recognized wine education standard — and has spent years studying European wine bar culture before bringing the concept home.

"Pique comes from the French 'piquer' — to provoke and spark curiosity. We want to make wine less intimidating and more enjoyable, allowing people to discover what they love in a relaxed, welcoming environment."

— Sasha Goenka, Founder, Pique

The wine list features around 12 selections by the glass and 24 by the bottle, with the entire lineup refreshed every month. That rotation is deliberate — it nudges regulars to try something new each visit rather than defaulting to the same Cabernet Sauvignon.

One standout is Pique's exclusive partnership with Nashik-based Vallonne Vineyards. The collaboration puts one of the few Indian orange wines currently available by the glass on the menu — a rarity in a country where most restaurants still limit their Indian wine offerings to a handful of familiar labels.

Sharing Plates With an Indian Soul

The food side of Pique draws on Goenka's collaboration with chef and cheesemaker Aditya Raghavan. The menu is European in inspiration but built on locally sourced Indian ingredients, designed for tables loaded with sharing plates rather than individual courses.

Dishes range from steak tartare with a smoked oyster emulsion to chicken Caesar pizza, a French onion grilled cheese, and a parmesan cheesecake finished with red wine reduction. The approach is comfort-forward — food meant to make a second glass of wine feel like the obvious next move.

Beyond Wine: Community and Culture

Pique is open all day from noon, positioning itself as a neighborhood anchor rather than a nightlife destination. The ground floor operates as a casual wine bar, while the upper level offers a more intimate dining experience.

The music programming swings from jazz and bossa nova on weeknights to Y2K and old-school hip-hop on themed evenings. Goenka is also planning a post-run drunch — a brunch concept tied to Mumbai's growing run-club community, betting that the city's fitness-obsessed millennials will trade their post-workout smoothies for a glass of something fermented.

What It Means for Indian Wine Culture

India's domestic wine market has grown steadily but remains a fraction of its beer and spirits sectors. Most wine consumption is concentrated in Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Goa, and the category has long struggled with perception problems — seen as either too expensive or too pretentious for everyday drinking.

Pique's bet is that the format matters as much as the product. European cities are dotted with neighborhood wine bars where a glass costs the same as a craft beer and nobody expects you to know the difference between Burgundy and Bordeaux. If Goenka can replicate that ease in Mumbai's financial district, it could signal a broader shift in how urban India drinks.
